source: Canairy's October 2026 family preparedness research. General information, not financial, legal or medical advice.
principles: Decide in calm times what moves you up a stage and what moves you down, then follow the rule even when the news feels louder than the numbers.
Areas can sit at different stages. Your whole household moves to Prepare only when two areas are there at once.
A stage you can't name a number for drops back on its own. Most alarms never become catastrophes.
Make leaving cheap and fast, but don't leave on rumors. People who did well in past crises acted early on signals they chose ahead of time.

ladder.name: Baseline
ladder.up: A reading past its watch line, or a dated tripwire within 30 days.
ladder.today: Know where documents, cash, water and lights are.
ladder.week: Two weeks of water, food and medicine; a documents kit; a written family plan.
ladder.month: Passports, a will, backups and an outage kit.
ladder.cost: $3,000 to $8,000 once, then about $300 a year

ladder.name: Watch
ladder.meaning: Something is off. Look closer, spend little.
ladder.up: A reading past its act line for 2 weeks, or a trigger for that area.
ladder.down: Every reading back inside its watch line for 30 days.
ladder.today: Check readings once a day, not every hour. Keep the tank above half.
ladder.week: Top up supplies, check passport dates, confirm the school's emergency plan.
ladder.month: Rehearse the plan; test the battery and the radio.

ladder.name: Prepare
ladder.meaning: Disruption is plausible in weeks to months.
ladder.up: A reading past its brace line, or an event trigger for that area.
ladder.today: Fill the cars, refill prescriptions early, bring home cash for 2 to 4 weeks of spending.
ladder.week: Supplies to 30 days; deposits spread across banks under FDIC limits; service the battery or generator.
ladder.month: Staples toward 90 days; review job risk; refresh the plan for a second place to stay.

ladder.name: Brace
ladder.meaning: An event is under way; local effects are likely within days. Both adults agree on the trigger, not the mood.
ladder.up: Officials order an evacuation, or home becomes unsafe.
ladder.down: An all-clear, and services normal for 7 days.
ladder.today: Cancel non-essential travel; keep an adult within 30 minutes of each child; go-bags in the car.
ladder.week: Start the family plan: who stays where.
ladder.month: Decide whether to move to the second place ahead of time.

ladder.name: Shelter or relocate
ladder.meaning: Home is unsafe or untenable. Set by officials or by you, never by readings.
ladder.down: Officials say it's safe and utilities have been back 72 hours.
ladder.today: Shelter in the basement, or leave by your first or second route.
ladder.week: Settle at the second place and keep income going.

ladder.name: Emergency
ladder.meaning: Act in minutes. Set by officials.
ladder.today: Get inside, stay inside, stay tuned. Call 911.

noRegret.title: A written family plan, a family safe word, an out-of-area contact, and local alerts
noRegret.why: Helps in every scenario. The safe word stops AI voice-clone scams: any urgent money request needs the word or a call back to a known number.

noRegret.title: A pact with nearby family or friends: a rally house, who picks up which child, shared supplies; plus a list of five neighbors
noRegret.why: Social ties predict who gets through a disaster better than gear does.

noRegret.title: Credit freezes for everyone, children included, and two hardware security keys per adult
noRegret.why: Blocks most identity theft and account takeovers, in good times and bad.

noRegret.title: Two weeks of water (a gallon per person per day), food you already eat, and medicine; 90-day prescriptions where allowed
noRegret.why: Covers storms, outages, illness waves, supply shocks and the first weeks of a blockade.

noRegret.title: Current passports for everyone, children included
noRegret.why: The longest lead time of any exit option: about 8 to 10 weeks. Children under 16 apply in person, usually with both parents.

noRegret.title: A will naming a guardian for your children, powers of attorney and health care proxies
noRegret.why: Helps in every scenario and costs the most to skip.

noRegret.title: An emergency fund (3 months; 6 to 9 if a job is exposed to AI), $1,000 to $2,000 in small bills, deposits under FDIC limits at two or more banks
noRegret.why: Card networks fail in outages, and bank freezes reward people who acted before they hit. FDIC covers $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category.

noRegret.title: Carbon monoxide alarms on every floor, smoke alarms, a first aid kit, and Stop the Bleed and CPR classes
noRegret.why: Portable generators kill nearly 100 people a year in the US through carbon monoxide.

noRegret.title: A 1 to 3 kWh battery power station and, with a basement, a battery backup sump pump
noRegret.why: Runs a fridge in cycles, the router, phones and lights with no carbon monoxide, and keeps the basement dry when the power is out.

noRegret.title: A fire-rated safe for originals, plus 3-2-1 backups: a local copy, a cloud copy and a drive kept somewhere else
noRegret.why: Protects records and income in fire, flood, ransomware and outages.

skip: Skip the $25,000 to $300,000 bunker, bulk gold and fear-driven buying. A basement corner with water, lights, a radio and two days of food gives most of the same protection, and solar plus a battery pays off every year.

1: Keep the tank above half and give the fuel budget some room.
2: Keep tanks three-quarters full.
Lock in heating fuel if you can, and charge the power station.
Ask about remote-work days.
3: Fill every tank and approved spare can; expect station lines.

1: Confirm deposits are under FDIC limits, and avoid borrowing to invest.
2: Hold 2 to 4 weeks of cash at home.
Open a second bank account.
Keep 6 to 12 months of expenses outside stocks, and don't panic-sell.
3: Live on cash. Insured US deposits have historically been paid within days.

1: Keep your résumé and portfolio current, renew licenses, and stay in touch with 20 people in your field.
2: Build the emergency fund toward 9 to 12 months.
Cut fixed costs and start one side income.
Learn to direct and check AI tools in your work.
3: File for unemployment in the first week.
Arrange health coverage (COBRA or your state marketplace).

1: Buy an extra week of the staples you already eat while prices are lower.
2: Build staples toward 90 days, eating the oldest first.
Check SNAP and WIC eligibility if money is tight.
3: Use the pantry first; panic-buying makes shortages worse.

1: Check that vaccines, including measles (MMR), are current, and keep masks on hand.
2: Get 90 days of key medicines and masks for everyone.
Build food to 30 days.
Plan remote work and a childcare bubble with family.
3: Limit contact, keep children home if schools close, and follow public health guidance.

1: Check supplies, charge devices, clear the sump pit, and know your flood zone.
2: Gas, cash, water and prescriptions; charge everything.
Photograph the house for insurance.
3: Fill a bathtub liner and set the freezer to its coldest.
Park away from trees and low ground.

1: Install pending updates on phones, computers and the router, and turn on two-step login.
2: Keep some cash and paper copies of key account numbers.
Download recent bank statements and check card activity weekly.
3: Expect outages of payments or power: use cash and watch for fraud.

1: Check passport dates, and buy electronics you were already planning to buy.
2: Get 90 days of prescriptions, staples toward 90 days, and 4 weeks of cash.
Review how much of your savings sits in chip and AI stocks.
Confirm your backups work.
3: Expect cyber disruption: charge batteries and fill fuel.
Stay close to the children, and choose which family house is the hub.

1: Passports for everyone, documents organized, and data-broker listings cleaned up.
2: Passports with 2+ years left.
Some Treasury bills held directly at TreasuryDirect, and an away fund on a card with no foreign fees.
Use end-to-end encrypted messaging, and don't post plans publicly.
3: Refundable travel options, records in encrypted storage you control, tight school pickup plans.

maintenance.what: Test alarms; charge the power station and radios; check the car kit; note each area's stage.
Rotate water and food; test the sump backup; restore one file from backup; check medicine dates; step down any stage you can't justify with a number.

maintenance.when: Twice a year, at the clock changes
maintenance.what: A lights-off evening on battery; a basement drill played as a game; resize the children's go-bag clothes.
Review insurance (flood, sewer backup rider), documents, passports (renew at 2 years left), the will and guardian, and the emergency fund's size.
